story_text.value:
Hi HN. Greg here.

I've been a full stack engineer for 20 years. Now all I do is shuffle messages between users, my agent fleet, our dev pipeline.. back and forth. I miss coding, solving problems, reasoning, and having an understanding and a mental model of all the work I'm juggling. But this is the job now, and there's no going back. I don't exactly feel like a 10x engineer yet, but I am for sure a 10-tab engineer.

I built (er, Claude built) Shufler to lean into my new reality. If the job is basically to shuffle things through a pipeline, why not have it be more fun.

Each row on the 3D gameboard is one of your existing terminal sessions. The columns are the steps your work moves through: Brainstorm, Plan, Build, QA, Review, Merge, Deploy. Your shipped PRs get stored in a warehouse/depot. The main things flowing across the board are your issues and PRs: each one rides along its session/row as it moves through review, CI and merge, and anything waiting on you turns red. I tend to manage several PRs within each Claude/Codex session, and this makes it easier for me to hold onto a mental model of where everything is. It's also made daily standups much easier to read-out.

I created a few skins/themes like a casino, a theme park, sky islands, a starship and a factory, because.. of course.

MacOS, works with Claude Code and Codex CLI, and cmux and iTerm (tmux should work, but I haven't tested it). It doesn't try to replace anything you already use.. just makes the orchestration more fun. You can still shift focus over to your terminal sessions when needed, use your existing skills, MCP servers, etc. There's a 3D library-building in each skin where you can specify your markdown/context folders or files, and then drag and drop to check them out by your rows/sessions.

I tried to be thoughtful on security, following patterns that I consider at work. No telemetry, and the only outside calls are your own gh calls to GitHub. Daemon only listens on localhost, and every action shows its command before it runs. MCP server is opt-in, and sending to other sessions is off by default; if you turn it on, every send is a preview plus a separate confirm you approve. Details are in the README's #safety-and-privacy, and the MCP threat model (including what it doesn't protect against) is in docs/MCP.md. To report a security issue privately (or contributions to improve), see SECURITY.md.

Demo with mock data, nothing to install at https://shufler.app

Repo at https://github.com/jgrichardson/shufler (MIT)

comment_text.value:
Ex-Googler here. I'm not sure there is one answer to your question.

The culture of your org is 100% dependent on where you are, and primarily flows from your Director. This is both good and bad.

The good: You can have islands of positive culture inside otherwise problematic organizations, provided the Director sets that positive culture and makes sure their managers and leaders help enforce it.

The bad: You can be one re-org away from that positive culture going away. That said, I experienced many higher-level re-orgs that people basically considered no-ops because our Director didn't change, and I know of orgs that have had good culture for over 10 years.

If you are considering a role in some part of Google (either as a new hire or an internal transfer), you should ask probing questions about the organization itself to try and understand its specific culture and how that culture is embraced by the people inside it.

comment_text.value:
> Net worth. It's a pretty good proxy.

TLDR; I have met quite a few very high net worth individuals, their spouses and offspring. Hundreds of them, actually. I have not been impressed overall with their intellectual capacity for learning important and lifesaving knowledge in preparation for life-changing natural survival conditions which are outside of their daily routine. The same has been true at the middle and lower income distributions under similar circumstances. I am neutral about the future IQ of the population of any of their descendants, poor or rich.. There are many other factors at play.

The long version:

That has not been my admittedly anecdotal experience among high, moderate, and average net work individuals and small to large congregations of those net worth groups in North, Central, South Americas, East Asia, the Pacific Islands, the UK and Northern Europe. I haven't found any specific factors resulting in concentration of above or below average IQ individuals within any of those groups. I have traveled much; been in direct leadership positions among high net worth individuals' on board of directors, and have been in direct contact with significant groups of low net worth populations in both labor and non-profit support roles. I do confess to not having conducted specific research in the IQ to net worth among those groups, so this is just an informed opinion.

So, I will yield on the sole point IFF net worth is assumed to be a strong proxy for high IQ; then we might be headed in a smarter direction in the portions of the general population resulting from those families. I do agree with the distinction that the proposed mechanism in the film Idiocracy is not what is occurring. It does however seem apparent that due to many different mechanisms we may be in for a significantly dumber future, and on that we also agree.

It may be that among the high net worth populations; there may be a factor within the high IQ subgroup that is aware of the complex difficulty for the planet due to excessive and wasteful overconsumption and the aggregate demand that additional population stresses the situation. That subgroup may be choosing to self deselect for reproduction, and that subgroup may be among the highest fraction of IQ. It doesn't appear that this aspect was in the study you referenced, nor in any of that study's sources' research. Did I miss that component

comment_text.value:
When I was growing up, for whatever reason, Leprosy was used as the outstanding example of a decease that completely incapacitated and made people social outcasts to the point they were sent off to islands to live with other Lepers. I don't know why this was culturally a big deal, I imagine it to be the same as quick sand for American children, just something adults were panicking way too much about. I am Mediterranean for context.

When I watched Mononoke, the scenes in the Iron Village completely befuddled me for a long time at first. This city both constantly establishes itself as a place with a deeply negative effect on the surrounding wilds. They're actively destroying the outskirts of the forest where a bunch of animal gods live, and yet at the same time, they're all nice, and oddly gender affirming and... The villain employs Lepers.

As in, they had nowhere else to go, so she took them in. And she has no problem taking a gun they built directly off their hands, completely unafraid. I grew learning that Lepers were being thrown out because everyone was afraid and they were highly contagious and no one knew what else to do, so having the villain, unironically, show the grace I learned belonged to "The modern world", was like a brick tossed directly inside my brain. She was the reason Ashitaka was dying, she was the reason the pig monster showed up. And yet, she was not a bad person.

Good art. Felt a lot of empathy for Ashitaka. Thought about it a lot, made me grow a lot. And all because someone in Japan, somehow, laser targeted me on my sensibilities on Leprosy. So random.

story_title.value: A Pig, the State, and War: Porco Rosso (Kurenai No Buta) (2014)

Here's a paper you can read and not just dismiss as something that I didn't read [1]. Some islands will vanish, some will grow, it's not as simple as everything is doomed everywhere. Have fun reading :)

> This record comprises 568 islands from 42 atolls spanning the western to the central Pacific Ocean from the Federated States of Micronesia, Marshall Islands, Kiribati and Tuvalu, and is one of the first robust attempts to statistically attribute the drivers of observed island changes within the past half-century. Our analyses demonstrate that island change and a range of its potential controls, including oceanographic, climatic and local-scale morphometric characteristics of reefs and islands, are not correlated, underscoring that no single variable could predict a uniform response across the study islands. The lack of association between sea-level rise and shoreline change on this large sample of islands addresses the common notion of a linear relationship between rising sea levels and magnitude of erosion in reef island systems.

> Analysis of 568 islands across the Pacific indicates that most islands have exhibited significant morphological changes over the timescale of analysis (1944–2018). Accretion was observed on 39% of transects, while 27% of transects showed erosion. Aggregated at the island scale, the balance of erosional and accretionary changes indicates a predominance of accretion on islands, with an average shoreline change of 0.51 m/decade resulting in a net expansion of 444.63 ha (~ 2.25%) of land area.

spa: a Vite SPA (React Router or SvelteKit in SPA mode) + a JSON API.

comment_text.value:
I come from northern Scotland. I've never really thought of it as one island. Even England has some notable ones like the Isle of Wight and Lindisfarne. (Wales and Northern Ireland have Anglesey and Rathlin.)

When you get to the Hebrides and Northern Isles, the scales are still pretty big. Most people don't realise that Shetland, for example, is a hundred miles from end to end (including Fair Isle).

It's also the best part of a hundred miles from Inverness to John O' Groats, and the road is bad beyond Easter Ross. Unlike the Faroe Islands, there has been little attempt to create tunnels... Just small bridges and causeways.

The smaller islands can get cut off in storms and power cuts come happen.

Knoydart and Moidart only used to be reachable by boat, despite being on the mainland. (You can walk but it's not easy.) They were so remote that the Protestant Reformation never reached them.

Even in the south west you have to factor in distance. For example, Campbelltown looks close to Glasgow on the map but takes at least three or four hours by bus. Tarbert to Campbelltown is thirty miles. The Isle of Jura to the west takes a long time to get to, unless you have a helicopter. (A shout to Galloway which is as far south as you can get in Scotland, and gets further south than Newcastle upon Tyne, but still has awful roads in many places.)

Places like Moidart, Knoydart, Kintyre, Glenelg, and even Cowal and Caithness function a bit like islands despite being on the mainland. Deliveries and utilities are horrible in these areas and they are being discriminated against by private delivery etc (the Royal Mail when it functioned better was a blessing to them.)

Of course there are parts of major continents which are much more remote, but these are bad enough. I've spent time in Australia where distances are incredible. Even Tasmania which looks small on the map is slightly smaller than Ireland.

You're free to make whatever mistaken assumptions you like about the kind of places I go and the kind of travel I do. You're wrong, obviously, but it's not like I can prove that any more than you can.

Some unlikely places where I've found Tabasco, though:

- at a cockfighting ring in rural Mindanao, Philippines.

- in a yurt camp in rural central Kyrgyzstan only accessible by horse

- at the galley on a Taiwanese container ship transiting the Panama canal

comment_text.value:
I don't love a lot of the design decisions sc2 made but at the end of the day it's pretty small nitpicking.

It's incredibly hard to divorce the map from the unit balance in a game like this and people eventually just settled on some combination of standard map features in order to balance around.

That being said, I think sc2 is considerably worse about map variety (mostly due to having more air units and more responsive/smaller collision box armies), every season bw had at least one "wacky" map pros were expected to play on, whether that involves islands or the nearly infinite number of tricks designers pulled off using minerals and gas geysers and such as ways to force certain play patterns

A couple of times they'd even design maps in such a way that one of your close expansion bases started off covered in creep, meaning zerg players could build there whenever they wantes but the other races had to destroy the creep first, with the idea being to make zerg stronger.

I think flying buildings are an interesting example of a fairly useful ability that ends up being extremely subtle, sort of like zerg healing. In almost any pro game, a terran player will lift off at least one building, frequently more (depending on how long the game lasts), but it's rarely a huge game defining moment, just a little optimization (unless they manage to lift off the barracks just when the speedlings show up...)

As you say, there's a balance between apm and "pure strategy", at one end you have chess and the other, dunno, bw I guess, and where you design for is going to involve a whole bunch of subjective factors.

story_title.value: Total Annihilation, rebuilt for modern computers

I agree the idea seems unrealistic. What's proposed sounds like fully automated luxury communism. Which is especially strange when promoted by the world's richest capitalist.

I guess the idea is that communism will actually work when central planning is managed by AI instead of people. Which, OK, maybe, but even if it's true, the question of how we get there from here without a violent revolution and/or the disempowerment of the human race seems unanswerable.

Elon talks about how the AI will saturate all human desires for material goods. And when I hear that I always think of Han Solo saying "I don't know, I can imagine quite a bit".

I can imagine that potentially mostly working for some goods like food and clothing and personal electronics, but without at least some pretty strict limits on what you're allowed to consume, a tiny minority could cause insane levels of waste. And as soon as you have limits you're going to get people trying to exploit them. That's just human nature.

Then for some other resources I can't see it working at all, chiefly land. Even if we accepted dramatic modification of the natural landscape, which we probably shouldn't, there will never be enough tropical islands or palatial ski chalets for everyone to own one for themselves.

story_text.value:
Since Railway getting pwned is getting all the attention right now, I thought now is a good time to showcase what we've been building. Stackdome is a self hosted platform as a service. The idea is to have simplicity of platforms like Railway and Render, but with the ability to run everything on infrastructure you control.

With Stackdome, you can deploy an application from GitHub, connect multiple services visually, add a managed database, create preview environments, and roll back the entire application if a release breaks.

Features:

- First class support for multi-service applications, shown on a canvas in the UI (inspired by Railway). You can edit, wire up, and create resources from the canvas.

- First class support for multiple clusters. Stackdome acts as the hub and places workloads across clusters (hub and spoke).

- Self hostable, from a small VPS to a large k8s cluster.

- Managed Postgres with WAL archiving, HA, backups, and PITR (CNPG underneath).

- A release system for the whole stack. A release targets everything, and you can roll it back if something breaks.

- Source to image, with an in cluster registry (Zot).

- Disposable preview environments, which can also be multi-service.

- Declarative apps via a Stackfile, deployed with the CLI.

Basically, the idea is to package the tooling in the CNCF/cloud-native ecosystem into an opinionated platform, so that developers can get a without being an expert in Kubernetes or a dozen other projects from the CNCF landscape.

Docs: https://docs.stackdome.com

story_text.value:
Hi HN, I'm Sanjay. I've been travelling since I moved from Pakistan to Stockholm in 2008; I live in Sydney now. My trips were scattered across a spreadsheet, airline apps, old inboxes and a photo library, so I built Trvlrr to hold all of it. It's how I plan all my future trips and look back at all my past ones. Forward a booking email (flights, trains, hotels, tours) to a private address and it lands on the right day of the right trip.

Every past trip is kept, with stats that count only what actually happened.

Photos are filed by trip and searchable by what's in them.

It's in Claude's and ChatGPT's and Raycast directories, so you can install it and use it via MCP: ask "when was I last in Lisbon or "add this hotel to my Japan trip". In fact, this is how I imported all of my travel history.

It's been a fun challenge working out the intricate details and adding features I'd always wanted in an app like this.

iPhone app plus a full web app (Android is under development). Free covers everything for few trips, you can add more via mcp to onboard but the app should be functional. No ads, no data selling.

Try without signing up: https://trvlrr.app/tools/countries-visited-map

I'd love for you to try it and send me any feedback you have.

Cheers, Sanjay

story_text.value:
This is my blog drawn as a network, with a light coat of paint to make it look like a video game map. Each city is a post, bigger cities have more incoming links, and roads are connections between posts. It updates semi-automatically every time I publish. (I used an LLM to write the code and drew about 90% of the art myself in Inkscape.)

For a long time I've been unsatisfied with the linear feeds and tag soups that most blogs use, so I decided to experiment with a non-linear view. I built some CLI tools that combine embedding similarity, LLM suggestions and human review to find the links between posts and quantify their strength. Now, every time I write a new piece, it takes me about 5 minutes to generate its links to/from older posts and grow the map accordingly.

The map is meant to look playful more than precise. For me, the key feature is how it enables making your own "journey" through the blog. The tricky part was finding a layout where closely related posts end up near each other AND the landscape doesn't change dramatically with every new post. I'm not a graph expert, but t-SNE on shortest-path distances over the link graph turned out to work well in my tests. Each update starts from the previous positions with early exaggeration off, and a Procrustes alignment keeps the map from rotating or drifting.

I hope it helps people get lost in there and find things they want to read. I'd like to see something like this on other blogs, so I'm sharing it here. I wonder if anyone else has tried similar ways to un-linearize their blogs.

story_text.value:
What’s up HN I'm Benji, and I’ve been building Frink since ~April this year.

Frink is a desktop-first, open-source (MIT) app for running coding agents in parallel and multi-step workflows that start on their own. It runs on your machine (macOS and Linux) with your own provider login. It currently supports Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Copilot, and OpenCode, but the latter 3 are in preview. No Frink account to use the app.

The biggest USP of Frink is workflows: think n8n for agents. You describe a routine in a sentence, for example: "every weekday at 9am, run the tests; if any fail, have an agent fix them, then wait for my approval before it opens a PR." Then, Frink builds it as a workflow (or simply, Flow): a list of steps you can read and change before it runs. A Flow can start on a schedule, from any webhook, or from an event from a third-party such as Linear, Shortcut, ClickUp, Sentry, PostHog, etc. Steps can be agent turns, shell commands, conditions, approval steps that stop and wait for you, or steps you write yourself in code (or ask the agent to write one). Everything that needs you (an approval, an agent's question, a finished task to review) lands in one Work Queue.

Other stuff:

* Up to four agents side by side, each on its own git worktree if you want. Or, many agents out of direct view.

* Every change shows as a diff; there's a code editor, a terminal, etc.

* Local-first: chats, Flows and tasks live in SQLite on your machine.

* Easier provider parity: currently working on and improving the tooling setup between providers. Once inside Frink, irrespective of what provider you use, the hooks, MCPs, and other tooling work out of the box between providers.

Why I built it: I started building it when there weren’t many other competitors; now the industry is swamped with ADEs and harnesses. However, in my opinion, each still lacks good automation for more fine-tuned scenarios. I doubled down on the flows to help me with my actual day-to-day job as a SWE, and over time it’s helped me automate most of the PRs being shipped across my personal projects, team, etc., to the point that it’s a continuous loop and helps a whole ton.

Notes: Windows isn't supported yet. Flows only run on Claude Code and Codex for now. It's a solo project, so expect sharp edges.

story_text.value:
I run long sessions with Claude. For a long time I've had Claude in the middle of some difficult coding task, and then I see the auto-compact message pop up. Every time I wonder if Claude actually picks everything up correctly and nothing is lost. Claude told me 78/82 auto-compactions landed while Claude was working. For a while I couldn't do much. At first I made a skill that would make Claude explicitly save progress throughout long runs. But that didn't fix the core problem and cost more tokens as well. Now that mods came out, I fixed the actual problem.

catnap tells Claude at 50% context what the context is and that it should finish what it's working on, write a handoff, and then initialize compaction itself. When Claude finishes its task, catnap compacts, and Claude can then pick up work again. The handoff replaces Claude Code's default summary, so we don't do similar work twice. If Claude for some reason doesn't compact before 60%, it gets a stricter note. And Claude Code's default auto-compact kicks in at 70% as a backstop. The 3 numbers are all settings.

After I took on catnap, 0 of 129 naps came mid-task: 98 of them in benchmarks and 31 in my own sessions.

The cost is the same as the default auto-compact kicking in at the same point, in tokens and dollars, on 200K and 1M context windows. Compared to the default auto-compaction that kicks in when context is nearly full, catnap used 56% fewer tokens. But lowering the default auto-compact will get you most of the way there as well.

I measured memory today as well. Claude worked through tasks one message at a time while 20 instructions and facts were said in the chat, inside long chatty messages, and nowhere else. Asked right after compaction to list them from memory, no file reads: all 20 were listed with catnap and with the default compaction, in every run (15 with catnap, 5 with the default). So in my tests the memory was exactly the same, but catnap got there with a handoff 60% shorter (4.0K tokens against 10K).

I was surprised that catnap is actually faster than the default option. This wasn't even one of the reasons I wanted to make this, it just happened. Since Claude writes the handoff in one go instead of the separate summary call the default makes, and the note is shorter, tasks finish sooner: measured end to end, 406 seconds instead of 464.

Try it with nothing installed:

  npx github:LippInc/catnap
It prints how often auto-compact cut in mid-task in your own logs (reads numbers only, sends nothing).

Install (needs Claude Code 2.1.287 or later, where mods are on by default):

  claude plugin marketplace add LippInc/catnap
  claude plugin install catnap@lippinc
Currently Claude Code only, tested on Windows and Linux. The memory test used made-up coding tasks on a 200K window.

Some related tools: compact-adviser, handoff-compact, session-pilot and sub-agent-compact. What catnap adds: Claude finishes its piece first, and the numbers on where the cut lands.

story_text.value:
I've been working on generative LEGO assembly models recently, but there are similar projects already, so I wanted to try some harder cases: specialized parts (incl. technic), multi-modal prompting (incl. using images, 3D meshes or almost any input), constrained inventory (so you could upload just parts you have), ensuring physical validity and generating buildable instructions, being able to tweak, modify or rebuild entirely an existing build etc.

TL;DR the pipeline got more complex than expected and I ended up with an agentic harness leveraging recursive program synthesis, combinatorial diffusion, semantic 3D search and operations on assembly hypergraphs.

Yet I am quite happy with the result. It should be able to handle as well a functional mechanism, LEGO robot, artistic landscape or fancy animal.

Most importantly, it also checks for subgraph matches of builds present in catalogue, being able to check (and possibly enforce) originality and prevent copying existing MOCs.

Have fun!

story_text.value:
TL;DR: 12 years ago I built a service that forwards simple HTML forms to an email address. I've been procrastinating on finishing it ever since, until today. You point your form at it and every submission lands in your inbox. It runs on credits, 1 credit = 1 message, no subscription. Perfect for static websites.

—

Hey folks, back around 2014, alongside my job as a software engineer, I was building a lot of static websites for my own clients, mostly small businesses that just wanted a simple site. To avoid headaches, I went fully static, often hosted on GitHub Pages and similar.

But most clients also wanted a contact form, and a form needs a server running somewhere. I had my own weekend-hacked service for this, which literally just forwarded the form to the client's email.

I didn't invent anything here: one service I particularly remember was FormKeep by thoughtbot, that I really liked.

So I started building my own, mostly because I loved losing myself in side projects like this, and also because I was a cheap ass and thought I could do something similar for less, and without a subscription.

By 2016 I had done about 90% of what I'm showing you today. I called it "The Great Forwarder". Everything was ready: backend, frontend, hosting, Stripe, landing page. I even had a designer friend help with the design (sorry, Valentin, if I've botched it since). Then I started another project, which took off right away and took all my attention for a while. Fun fact: that project has been using this service ever since, and almost every message ever sent through it came from there.

So for years, I kept Forwarder.cc up to date, upgrading libraries and trying new ones: axios, got, Redux, Zustand, create-react-app, webpack, Vite… It became my laboratory for everything I wanted to explore, while always staying up and maintained (again, for my own use only).

The only thing that ever held me back from launching it was a missing help center, and, more honestly, the fear of putting it in front of people.

So today's the day: after 12 years of procrastination, I finally finished the help center.

I know there are a ton of similar services nowadays, but anyway, what do you think of that help center
